lessons.title: IoT Fundamentals, Architecture and Data Flow
lessons.overview: The Internet of Things (IoT) connects physical devices that sense, compute and exchange data so useful actions can be taken. A useful IoT solution is not just a sensor or an app: it is the complete path from a real-world event to measurement, communication, processing, and a decision.
objectives: Explain: Thing/device: a physical object with sensing, control or communication capability.
Explain: Sensor measures a physical quantity such as temperature, light or moisture; actuator changes the physical environment, such as opening a valve.
Explain: Device → network/gateway → processing/storage → dashboard/automation is a common end-to-end flow.
Explain: An edge device processes data near the sensor; cloud services collect data for remote access and larger-scale analytics.
prerequisites: Understanding of the prior unit and basic computer/electronics concepts
keyConcepts: Thing/device: a physical object with sensing, control or communication capability.
Sensor measures a physical quantity such as temperature, light or moisture; actuator changes the physical environment, such as opening a valve.
Device → network/gateway → processing/storage → dashboard/automation is a common end-to-end flow.
An edge device processes data near the sensor; cloud services collect data for remote access and larger-scale analytics.
Publish/subscribe decouples senders and receivers; request/response is an alternative communication pattern.
IoT design must consider power, connectivity, security, reliability, latency and maintenance from the beginning.
formulas: Measurement-to-action loop: sense → validate → transmit → decide → act → confirm

lessons.theory:
## What makes a system IoT?
An ordinary electronic sensor is not automatically an IoT system. A typical IoT system has a physical process, a device reading a sensor, a communication path and a software service/application that makes measurements useful. Remote access and automatic decisions are common, but not every application requires a public cloud.

## Functional layers
**Perception/device layer** collects physical values. **Network layer** transports information using wired or wireless methods. **Processing/platform layer** validates, stores and analyses it. **Application layer** displays information and controls actions. Security and device management apply across every layer.

## Example: water tank monitor
An ultrasonic level sensor measures the tank. A microcontroller converts the reading into a percentage and sends it over Wi-Fi. A dashboard shows the current level, while a rule issues an alert below a threshold. If an automated pump is added, a relay driver/contactor—never a GPIO pin directly—switches the pump. Add manual override and a safety cut-off.

## Edge versus cloud
Edge processing reduces communication and latency; cloud processing helps with aggregation, backups and reporting. A robust device should behave safely if the internet connection fails.

lessons.title: Sensors, Actuators, Controllers and Safe Wiring
lessons.overview: Hardware makes an IoT idea real. Learn how sensors differ from actuators, when to choose a microcontroller or a single-board computer, and how power levels, analog signals and driver circuits affect a reliable prototype.
objectives: Explain: Digital sensors provide already encoded data or discrete states; analog sensors produce a continuous voltage/current related to a physical quantity.
Explain: An ADC converts an analog signal into a digital representation; many microcontrollers include ADC channels, while traditional Raspberry Pi GPIO lacks built-in general-purpose analog input.
Explain: Microcontrollers such as Arduino/ESP32 run small dedicated firmware; Raspberry Pi is a Linux single-board computer suited to multitasking, networking and local services.
Explain: A transistor/MOSFET driver or relay module is needed for loads exceeding GPIO voltage/current limits.
prerequisites: Understanding of the prior unit and basic computer/electronics concepts
keyConcepts: Digital sensors provide already encoded data or discrete states; analog sensors produce a continuous voltage/current related to a physical quantity.
An ADC converts an analog signal into a digital representation; many microcontrollers include ADC channels, while traditional Raspberry Pi GPIO lacks built-in general-purpose analog input.
Microcontrollers such as Arduino/ESP32 run small dedicated firmware; Raspberry Pi is a Linux single-board computer suited to multitasking, networking and local services.
A transistor/MOSFET driver or relay module is needed for loads exceeding GPIO voltage/current limits.
Power budgeting includes idle and peak current consumption, regulator efficiency and battery life.
I2C shares clock/data among addressed devices; SPI normally uses clock/data plus chip-select; UART is asynchronous point-to-point serial.

lessons.theory:
## How to choose a controller
Use a low-power microcontroller for simple real-time sampling/control, especially on a battery. Use a Raspberry Pi when you need Linux applications, camera processing, a local web service or more demanding computation. The best choice depends on power, boot time, performance and I/O requirements—not brand popularity.

## Sensor chain
A temperature, light or moisture measurement becomes useful after reading the sensor correctly, applying calibration if necessary, handling errors/out-of-range readings and adding units/timestamps. Analog sensors require conversion, either on the controller or an external ADC.

## Electrical safety
GPIO pins are logic signals, not power outlets. Share a reference ground when compatible, level-shift mismatched voltages, use resistors with LEDs, and use a transistor/driver plus flyback diode for inductive DC loads. For mains voltage, use a properly rated isolated module and qualified supervision; do not wire mains directly on a breadboard.

## Reliability
Add sensor fault detection (disconnected/implausible values), watchdog/restart strategy, secure enclosures and a safe output state after power loss.

lessons.title: Raspberry Pi Architecture, GPIO and Pinout
lessons.overview: Raspberry Pi is a family of small Linux computers. It combines a processor, RAM, storage interfaces, USB/display/network hardware and programmable GPIO. The 40-pin header provides general I/O, power, ground and alternate interfaces, but it is important to distinguish physical pin numbers from GPIO numbering.
objectives: Explain: SoC (System on a Chip) contains the processor and integrated controllers; memory and connectors vary between Pi models.
Explain: A standard 40-pin header includes 3.3 V and 5 V power pins, multiple ground pins, and 3.3 V-logic GPIO signals.
Explain: Physical pin number is the location on the header; BCM GPIO number names the SoC signal. They are not interchangeable.
Explain: I2C typically uses GPIO2 (SDA, physical pin 3) and GPIO3 (SCL, physical pin 5) on 40-pin Pis.
prerequisites: Understanding of the prior unit and basic computer/electronics concepts
keyConcepts: SoC (System on a Chip) contains the processor and integrated controllers; memory and connectors vary between Pi models.
A standard 40-pin header includes 3.3 V and 5 V power pins, multiple ground pins, and 3.3 V-logic GPIO signals.
Physical pin number is the location on the header; BCM GPIO number names the SoC signal. They are not interchangeable.
I2C typically uses GPIO2 (SDA, physical pin 3) and GPIO3 (SCL, physical pin 5) on 40-pin Pis.
SPI0 commonly uses GPIO10 MOSI, GPIO9 MISO, GPIO11 SCLK and GPIO8 CE0.
GPIO14 TXD and GPIO15 RXD commonly provide a UART interface; alternate functions can differ by OS/model configuration.

lessons.theory:
## Identify the parts
On a common Raspberry Pi board, identify the SoC, RAM, microSD boot/storage slot (model dependent), USB ports, display interface, network connector/radio, power input and GPIO header. Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 5 have different processors and board controllers; do not assume their performance, connectors or software interfaces are identical.

## Header numbering
**Physical pin numbering** counts positions on the 40-pin connector; **BCM numbering** names GPIO lines. For example, physical pin 11 corresponds to BCM GPIO17 on the usual 40-pin layout. Most modern Python examples use BCM chip line names.

## Voltage rules
The GPIO input/output logic is **3.3 V** and is generally **not 5 V tolerant**. The fact that the header has 5 V supply pins does *not* mean a GPIO input can safely receive 5 V. Protect inputs using a compatible sensor or proper level shifter.

## Hardware interfaces
GPIO supports digital input/output, while I2C/SPI/UART are ways to communicate with smart sensors/modules. Model-specific pin muxing and permissions must be configured and tested. Turn power off before changing wiring.

codeExamples.title: Button controls an LED (gpiozero)
codeExamples.code:
from gpiozero import LED, Button
from signal import pause

led = LED(17)         # BCM GPIO17, with resistor
button = Button(27)   # BCM GPIO27

button.when_pressed = led.on
button.when_released = led.off

try:
    pause()
finally:
    led.off()
codeExamples.explanation: GPIO17 drives a current-limited LED through a resistor and GPIO27 reads a correctly wired button. `pause()` keeps event handlers active; `finally` forces the LED off on exit. Always verify pin mapping and wiring before running.

commonMistakes: Using a direct motor/relay coil connection instead of a driver
Running a loop with no pause and wasting CPU
Forgetting exception handling for disconnected sensors
Hardcoding passwords/tokens in public scripts
examTips: Explain each imported module and every pin number
State which pins are inputs and outputs and the exact circuit assumptions

lessons.theory:
## Basic setup
Install a supported Raspberry Pi OS, enable required hardware interfaces and confirm your Python environment has a GPIO library compatible with your Pi model and OS. `gpiozero` offers simple device abstractions; its backend may need configuration on different devices.

## Blink and button
Connect an LED through an appropriate resistor to a GPIO and ground. A button can be connected using the library's internal pull-up assumptions or a documented external circuit. In `gpiozero`, an LED object provides `on()`/`off()` and a Button object provides `is_pressed` or callback handlers.

## Read–validate–act
For sensors, convert the raw measurement to a meaningful unit, test plausible ranges, handle timeouts, then send/store results. Do not trust one noisy measurement to control an important actuator. Add hysteresis or multiple-sample confirmation.

## Network requests
If sending data with an HTTP library, use TLS, a sensible timeout and a stored token—never embed a production secret into a public source file. Queue or retry data when offline but cap retries/backlog.

lessons.title: IoT Communication: MQTT, HTTP, I2C, SPI and Wireless
lessons.overview: IoT systems use different protocols for short on-board connections and remote networks. Pick protocols by traffic pattern, power consumption, range, bandwidth, latency and reliability—not by simply selecting the newest technology.
objectives: Explain: MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol with topics, publishers, subscribers and a broker.
Explain: HTTP is request/response and is convenient for dashboards, REST APIs and occasional device uploads.
Explain: CoAP is a compact REST-like protocol often run over UDP in constrained-device networks.
Explain: I2C is a clocked two-wire bus (SDA/SCL) with addressed devices and pull-up requirements.
prerequisites: Understanding of the prior unit and basic computer/electronics concepts
keyConcepts: MQTT is a lightweight publish/subscribe messaging protocol with topics, publishers, subscribers and a broker.
HTTP is request/response and is convenient for dashboards, REST APIs and occasional device uploads.
CoAP is a compact REST-like protocol often run over UDP in constrained-device networks.
I2C is a clocked two-wire bus (SDA/SCL) with addressed devices and pull-up requirements.
SPI commonly uses SCLK, MOSI, MISO and chip-select wires; suitable for faster peripheral exchanges.
UART uses asynchronous TX/RX (and shared ground) with matching baud settings.
Wi-Fi favors local high-bandwidth networking; BLE suits short-range low-energy links; LoRa/LoRaWAN enables long-range low-bitrate links.

lessons.theory:
## Separate local buses from internet protocols
**I2C, SPI and UART** commonly connect a controller to sensors/displays/modems over short distances. **MQTT, HTTP and CoAP** move application messages between networked endpoints. **Wi-Fi, BLE and LoRa** are wireless link technologies. These layers can coexist in one system.

## MQTT example
A soil sensor node publishes a reading to topic `farm/plot1/moisture`. A dashboard subscribes to that topic through a broker and receives readings. Topics are structured strings; they are not encryption or authorization. Use transport encryption, topic ACLs, identity and authentication.

## MQTT delivery levels
QoS 0 is at-most-once, QoS 1 is at-least-once (duplicates possible) and QoS 2 is exactly-once within MQTT delivery semantics (more overhead). A device application still needs to make commands idempotent as appropriate.

## Protocol selection
Use I2C for several addressed sensors on a board, SPI for suitable fast peripherals, UART for serial modules, MQTT for frequent asynchronous telemetry, and HTTP for request/response APIs. Consider network failure/reconnect behavior before deployment.

lessons.title: IoT Case Studies, Security and End-to-End Design
lessons.overview: A useful IoT case study connects a measurable real-world problem to hardware, communication, analysis and a safe action. Smart agriculture, homes, healthcare monitoring, factories and smart cities all use similar patterns but have different safety, privacy and reliability needs.
objectives: Explain: Smart irrigation: soil-moisture sensing, sensor validation, controller decision, valve/pump driver and dashboard logs.
Explain: Industrial condition monitoring: temperature/vibration readings, time-series patterns and maintenance alerts.
Explain: Smart home: presence/lighting/climate control with local fallback and user override.
Explain: Healthcare monitoring requires stricter privacy, validation and clinical oversight; hobby prototypes must not be treated as medical devices.
prerequisites: Understanding of the prior unit and basic computer/electronics concepts
keyConcepts: Smart irrigation: soil-moisture sensing, sensor validation, controller decision, valve/pump driver and dashboard logs.
Industrial condition monitoring: temperature/vibration readings, time-series patterns and maintenance alerts.
Smart home: presence/lighting/climate control with local fallback and user override.
Healthcare monitoring requires stricter privacy, validation and clinical oversight; hobby prototypes must not be treated as medical devices.
Threats include default passwords, exposed brokers, insecure firmware updates and stored personal data leaks.
Secure-by-design includes strong identity, least privilege, encrypted transport, OTA update verification and logging.
Reliability requires offline behavior, watchdogs, safe actuator defaults and sensor-failure detection.

practiceQuestions.question: A safe automated irrigation system should prevent:
Which practice is most secure?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Authentication, least privilege and encryption are core protections.

lessons.theory:
## Case study 1: smart irrigation
Problem: a farm wastes water due to fixed schedules. A soil-moisture sensor sends calibrated readings to a controller; the controller checks both dryness and whether the tank has water. A driver controls the pump/valve. Telemetry is published to a dashboard for history and alerts. Add minimum run/rest times, manual override and fault shutdown. The rule must not activate a dry-running pump.

## Case study 2: machine-health monitoring
Attach appropriate vibration and temperature sensors to machines, record readings with timestamps, and compare with a normal baseline. Send alerts for sustained anomalies rather than individual noise spikes. Treat an alert as diagnostic evidence, not automatic proof that a machine will fail.

## Case study 3: room monitoring
Measure occupancy and temperature, adjust lighting or ventilation, and retain a local wall switch override. Minimize storing identifying location data and protect management endpoints.

## Security checklist
Use unique credentials per device, restrict network access, encrypt traffic, rotate credentials safely, validate cloud commands, and sign firmware updates. For real actuators, enforce a **local hardware/software safety envelope** so a malicious or incorrect network command cannot bypass physical limits.

## How to present an exam case study
Write problem → objectives → block diagram → hardware → software/protocol → working steps → benefits → limitations/safety. This answers more marks than naming devices alone.

Smart agriculture, homes, healthcare monitoring, factories and smart cities all use similar patterns but have different safety, privacy and reliability needs. Review the comparison table and diagram, then explain each part in your own words.
cheatSheet: Smart irrigation: soil-moisture sensing, sensor validation, controller decision, valve/pump driver and dashboard logs.
Industrial condition monitoring: temperature/vibration readings, time-series patterns and maintenance alerts.
Smart home: presence/lighting/climate control with local fallback and user override.
Healthcare monitoring requires stricter privacy, validation and clinical oversight; hobby prototypes must not be treated as medical devices.
Threats include default passwords, exposed brokers, insecure firmware updates and stored personal data leaks.

vivaBank.question: Difference between IoT and a standalone embedded system?
vivaBank.modelAnswer: An IoT system connects physical devices for exchanging data/remote coordination, whereas an embedded system can work completely standalone.

vivaBank.question: Why does Raspberry Pi often need an external ADC?
vivaBank.modelAnswer: Its usual GPIO header does not provide direct general-purpose analog-to-digital inputs.

vivaBank.question: What is MQTT?
vivaBank.modelAnswer: A lightweight broker-based publish/subscribe messaging protocol used for asynchronous telemetry and commands.
